source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's NVA5-NVA7 campus in Sterling, Virginia publishes 116 MW of IT capacity, the third largest published figure of any facility mapped in the state.

Virginia has 376 mapped data centers but only 29 that publish a megawatt figure. That gap is the more important fact. Most of the state's data center footprint is invisible at the megawatt level, and this campus is one of the few that is not. Its 116 MW is roughly 4.5 percent of the 2,563.4 MW of published capacity in Virginia, a share derived from the two numbers rather than claimed by the operator.

The 116 MW is a capacity number, not a consumption number. The operator publishes no rack count, accelerator count, or power usage effectiveness on the spec page read here, so translating it to AI workloads requires an assumption. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 116 MW is roughly 2,900 racks. At 10 kW per rack, typical of older enterprise colocation, it is roughly 11,600. Neither is CyrusOne's claim, and the split between training and traditional colocation at this site is not published. What the figure does establish is that the campus is sized for a meaningful share of a regional grid's load, and that electrical capacity, not building shell, is the number that matters.

The certifications field is empty, so nothing is published about what standards this campus has been qualified against. That absence limits what can be said, and is not evidence that no certifications exist. The address and postal code are also unpublished, so the campus can be placed in Sterling, Virginia, and no more precisely. The case for this campus mattering to AI rests on the 116 MW and its rank, both published, and on the rack-level composition, which is not.
